"All sides have used indiscriminate force as a matter of routine, and in 2008 violence has taken on a new dimension with the targeted murders of aid workers and civil society activists," the report states. "The human rights and humanitarian catastrophe facing Somalia today threatens the lives and livelihoods of millions of Somalis on a scale not witnessed since the early 1990s." Heavy fighting in Mogadishu and across Somalia has driven more than a million people from their homes. (CNN) — The United States and other Western powers have “exacerbated Somalia’s downward spiral” and must reassess their policies in the East African country, a Human Rights Watch report has warned.

A recent image shows Islamist fighters at a camp on the northern outskirts of Mogadishu.

The report, released Monday, blames policies pursued under President George W. Bush for “breeding the very extremism that [they are] supposed to defeat.”

“The new administration of U.S. President Barack Obama should urgently review U.S. policy in Somalia and the broader Horn of Africa and break with the failed approach of his predecessor,” the report said.

It also criticizes key European governments for failing “to address the human rights dimensions of the crisis, with many officials hoping that somehow unfettered support to abusive TFG [Somali transitional government] forces will improve stability.”

Somalia’s weak transitional government, backed by Ethiopian forces, continues to battle Islamic militias, with the fighting concentrated in the capital, Mogadishu. Ethiopian forces have not withdrawn from the country, as required under a recent cease-fire agreement.

Ethiopia invaded Somalia two years ago and successfully routed the Islamic militia that had seized control of the capital. The Human Rights Watch report states that the United States “directly backed Ethiopia’s intervention.”

Since the 2006 overthrow of the Islamic Courts Union, Somalia has endured “unconstrained warfare and violent rights abuses” by all warring parties.

“All sides have used indiscriminate force as a matter of routine, and in 2008 violence has taken on a new dimension with the targeted murders of aid workers and civil society activists,” the report states.

“The human rights and humanitarian catastrophe facing Somalia today threatens the lives and livelihoods of millions of Somalis on a scale not witnessed since the early 1990s.”

Heavy fighting in Mogadishu and across Somalia has driven more than a million people from their homes. The lawlessness has also spilled into the waters off the Horn of Africa, where international vessels are routinely hijacked by suspected Somali pirates demanding large ransoms.

Human Rights Watch offers specific recommendations to the Somali and Ethiopian governments, the main militias, and the international community to address human rights abuses. It calls on the West to “insist upon an end to the impunity that has fueled the worst abuses — and the right place to start is by moving the U.N. Security Council to establish a Commission of Inquiry to document abuses and lay the groundwork for accountability.”

Journalist Abdinasir Mohamed Guled contributed to this report.
outputs.L2:
(CNN) — A report from Human Rights Watch has cautioned that the United States and other Western governments have worsened Somalia’s decline and need to rethink their approach to the East African nation.

The report, issued Monday, says policies pursued under President George W. Bush helped create “the very extremism” they were intended to combat. It urged the administration of President Barack Obama to quickly reassess U.S. strategy toward Somalia and the wider Horn of Africa, and to abandon what it described as the failed policies of the previous administration.

The report also criticizes major European governments, saying they have not dealt with the human rights aspects of the crisis. It says many officials appear to believe that giving unrestricted support to abusive forces of Somalia’s Transitional Federal Government, or TFG, will somehow bring greater stability.

Somalia’s fragile transitional government, supported by Ethiopian troops, is still fighting Islamist militias, with much of the combat centered in the capital, Mogadishu. Ethiopian forces remain inside Somalia despite a recent cease-fire agreement requiring their withdrawal.

Ethiopia entered Somalia militarily two years earlier and defeated the Islamist militia that had taken over Mogadishu. According to Human Rights Watch, the United States “directly backed Ethiopia’s intervention.”

Since the Islamic Courts Union was overthrown in 2006, Somalia has experienced unchecked warfare and severe human rights violations committed by all sides in the conflict, the report says. It states that indiscriminate force has been used routinely by every party, and that in 2008 the violence expanded to include targeted killings of aid workers and civil society activists.

Human Rights Watch warns that Somalia’s current human rights and humanitarian emergency is endangering the lives and means of survival of millions of Somalis on a scale not seen since the early 1990s.

Intense fighting in Mogadishu and elsewhere in Somalia has forced more than one million people to flee their homes. The country’s instability has also spread into waters off the Horn of Africa, where suspected Somali pirates frequently seize international ships and demand large ransom payments.

The Human Rights Watch report lays out recommendations for the Somali and Ethiopian governments, leading militias, and the international community on how to confront human rights abuses. It urges Western governments to demand an end to the impunity behind the gravest violations, saying an appropriate first step would be for the U.N. Security Council to create a Commission of Inquiry to record abuses and prepare the way for accountability.

Journalist Abdinasir Mohamed Guled contributed to the report.
outputs.L3:
Human Rights Watch warned that U.S. and Western policies have worsened the crisis in Somalia and helped fuel the very extremism they were intended to defeat. According to the organization, international efforts focused primarily on counterterrorism and short-term security goals have contributed to instability, strengthened militant recruitment, and deepened the suffering of civilians.

In its report, Human Rights Watch urged President Barack Obama’s administration to conduct an urgent review of U.S. policy toward Somalia and the wider Horn of Africa. The group argued that Washington should reassess strategies that rely heavily on military action, proxy forces, and support for abusive allies, and instead place greater emphasis on human rights, civilian protection, accountability, and long-term political solutions.

European governments also came under criticism. Human Rights Watch accused them of overlooking serious human rights concerns while providing political and material support to Somalia’s transitional government forces. These forces, the report said, were responsible for abuses against civilians, yet Western governments continued to back them in the hope that they could help restore stability and counter Islamist armed groups.

At the time, Somalia’s transitional government, supported by Ethiopian troops, was continuing to fight Islamic militias despite a cease-fire agreement that called for the withdrawal of Ethiopian forces. The continued fighting undermined efforts to achieve a political settlement and contributed to further insecurity across the country.

The report emphasized that all sides in Somalia’s conflict had committed serious abuses, including indiscriminate attacks and other violations of international humanitarian law. Civilians bore the brunt of the violence, with many killed, injured, or forced to flee their homes. Human Rights Watch described the situation as a humanitarian catastrophe, noting that more than one million people had been displaced by the conflict.

In a report on the conflict, the organization says that strong international backing for Somalia’s Transitional Federal Government, combined with support for Ethiopia’s military intervention, has contributed to escalating violence and widespread abuses against civilians.

According to Human Rights Watch, Western governments have focused too narrowly on counterterrorism and on defeating Islamist armed groups, while failing to confront serious human rights violations committed by their allies. The organization urges the Obama administration and European governments to reassess their approach and to stop supporting policies that overlook abuses by Somali government forces, Ethiopian troops, and other allied actors.

The report describes a conflict marked by indiscriminate attacks, targeted killings, arbitrary arrests, and the destruction of civilian neighborhoods. It says that fighting in Mogadishu and other areas has forced hundreds of thousands of people from their homes, producing Somalia’s worst humanitarian emergency since the famine and civil war of the early 1990s. Civilians, the report argues, have borne the overwhelming burden of the violence, with many trapped between abusive government forces, foreign troops, insurgent groups, and clan militias.

Human Rights Watch also warns that current international policies may be counterproductive. By backing abusive forces and failing to demand accountability, Western governments risk strengthening the very extremist movements they seek to weaken. The report argues that civilian suffering, impunity, and resentment toward foreign intervention have helped armed opposition groups recruit supporters and portray themselves as defenders against outside aggression.

The organization calls for a major shift in policy. It urges the United States and European governments to make human rights protection central to their engagement in Somalia, press all parties to the conflict to end abuses, and ensure accountability for violations of international humanitarian law. Without such changes, Human Rights Watch warns, international support for Somalia’s transitional authorities and Ethiopia’s intervention will continue to fuel instability, radicalization, and humanitarian catastrophe.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a CNN-style news article about a Human Rights Watch report criticizing U.S. and Western policy in Somalia under George W. Bush and urging Barack Obama to change course.
counterfactuals.output:
**Human Rights Watch urges Obama to shift U.S. policy in Somalia**

**WASHINGTON (CNN)** — Human Rights Watch sharply criticized U.S. and Western policy toward Somalia during the George W. Bush administration, saying counterterrorism priorities helped fuel abuses and instability in the Horn of Africa nation, and urged President Barack Obama to take a different approach.

In a report released as the Obama administration was taking shape, the rights group said Washington and its allies focused too heavily on defeating suspected Islamist militants while failing to adequately address abuses by Somalia’s transitional government, Ethiopian forces and other armed groups.

Human Rights Watch said U.S. support for Ethiopia’s 2006 military intervention in Somalia and backing for Somalia’s weak transitional government contributed to a climate in which civilians were trapped between insurgents, government forces and foreign troops. The group also criticized Western governments for supporting counterterrorism operations that it said included unlawful detentions, renditions and cooperation with abusive security forces in the region.

“Somalia has been treated as a battlefield in the war on terror, and ordinary Somalis have paid the price,” the report said in substance, calling for a policy based more strongly on human rights, accountability and protection of civilians.

The group urged the Obama administration to review U.S. security assistance and intelligence cooperation in Somalia and neighboring countries, press Somali authorities and regional partners to end abuses, and support investigations into alleged war crimes by all sides.

Somalia has been without an effective central government since 1991. The collapse of state institutions gave rise to clan militias, warlords, Islamist movements and, later, the militant group al-Shabaab. Ethiopian troops entered Somalia in late 2006 to oust the Islamic Courts Union, a movement that had taken control of much of southern Somalia, including Mogadishu. The United States backed Ethiopia’s action, arguing that Islamist militants in Somalia posed a regional and international security threat.

Human Rights Watch said the aftermath of the intervention was disastrous for civilians. Fighting in Mogadishu and other areas displaced hundreds of thousands of people, and rights groups documented indiscriminate shelling, arbitrary arrests and attacks on civilians. Insurgent groups were also accused of targeted killings, suicide bombings and using populated areas for military operations.

The report said Western governments, including the United States, should not ignore abuses committed by allies in the name of counterterrorism. It called on the Obama administration to make respect for human rights a central condition of U.S. engagement in Somalia.

The Bush administration had defended its Somalia policy as necessary to prevent al Qaeda-linked militants from using the country as a safe haven. U.S. officials also pointed to humanitarian assistance and diplomatic support for Somalia’s transitional institutions.

But Human Rights Watch argued that the policy failed even on its own security terms, helping to deepen resentment and strengthen extremist groups.

The group said Obama had an opportunity to reset U.S. policy by backing accountable governance, humanitarian access and civilian protection, while ensuring that counterterrorism operations comply with international law.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.output:
**Human Rights Watch: Western Backing Has Worsened Somalia Crisis**

Human Rights Watch has warned that Western support for Ethiopia and Somalia’s Transitional Federal Government has intensified Somalia’s conflict and deepened the country’s human rights crisis.

In a report, the rights group said military, diplomatic and financial backing from the United States, European governments and other allies helped sustain policies that contributed to widespread abuses against civilians. Human Rights Watch argued that international efforts aimed at combating terrorism and strengthening Somalia’s transitional authorities instead fueled violence, displacement and impunity.

The group said Ethiopian forces, which entered Somalia to support the transitional government against Islamist insurgents, were implicated in indiscriminate attacks, killings, arbitrary detentions and other abuses. It also accused forces loyal to Somalia’s transitional authorities and insurgent groups of committing serious violations, including attacks in populated areas that placed civilians at grave risk.

According to Human Rights Watch, Western governments focused too heavily on security concerns and counterterrorism objectives while failing to hold their allies accountable for abuses. The organization said this approach undermined prospects for peace and alienated Somali civilians, many of whom have suffered through years of lawlessness, factional fighting and humanitarian collapse.

Somalia has been without a strong central government since 1991. The Transitional Federal Government, formed with international backing, has struggled to establish authority beyond limited areas and has depended heavily on foreign support. Ethiopia’s intervention, intended to bolster the government and weaken Islamist forces, sparked fierce resistance and contributed to prolonged urban warfare, particularly in Mogadishu.

Human Rights Watch called on Western governments to reassess their policies, condition assistance on respect for human rights, and press all parties to the conflict to end abuses against civilians. It also urged stronger support for accountability measures and humanitarian access.

The warning comes amid continued instability in Somalia, where civilians remain trapped between government forces, foreign troops, insurgent groups and clan militias. Aid agencies have repeatedly reported mass displacement, food shortages and limited access to medical care, raising fears that the conflict could further deteriorate unless international policy changes.

counterfactuals.output:
I can’t write it as an actual CNN article or imply CNN published it, but here is a CNN-style news summary:

---

## Human Rights Watch urges U.N. inquiry into abuses in Somalia conflict

Human Rights Watch is calling for an independent United Nations investigation into alleged war crimes and human rights abuses committed during Somalia’s long-running conflict, saying civilians have borne the brunt of violence involving Somali government forces, Ethiopian troops, Islamist militias and other armed groups.

In a new report, the rights organization describes widespread abuses during and after Ethiopia’s military intervention in Somalia, which began in late 2006 in support of the internationally backed Transitional Federal Government. The intervention ousted the Islamic Courts Union from Mogadishu but helped fuel a bloody insurgency led by Islamist militias, including groups that later evolved into or aligned with al-Shabaab.

Human Rights Watch says all sides in the conflict have violated the laws of war. Ethiopian and Somali government forces are accused of indiscriminate attacks, arbitrary detention, torture and mistreatment of civilians. Islamist insurgents are accused of targeted killings, executions, forced recruitment and attacks launched from densely populated neighborhoods, exposing civilians to retaliation.

The report also criticizes the role of the United States, saying Washington supported Ethiopia’s intervention and backed Somali government forces as part of its broader counterterrorism strategy in the Horn of Africa. Human Rights Watch argues that U.S. policy focused heavily on security concerns while failing to press allies strongly enough over abuses against civilians.

The conflict has devastated Somalia’s capital and displaced large numbers of people. Human Rights Watch says hundreds of thousands fled Mogadishu during waves of fighting, many ending up in overcrowded camps with limited access to food, clean water and medical care. Aid agencies have repeatedly warned that insecurity and attacks on humanitarian workers have made it difficult to reach displaced communities.

The report places Somalia’s internal violence in the context of a wider regional crisis. Ethiopia’s military involvement deepened political divisions inside Somalia and drew condemnation from many Somalis who viewed the intervention as an occupation. Meanwhile, Islamist militias used that anger to recruit fighters and portray themselves as a resistance movement.

Human Rights Watch also notes that Somalia’s lawlessness has contributed to the rise of piracy off the country’s coast. With no effective central government for years, armed pirate networks have operated from coastal areas, hijacking commercial vessels and demanding ransom payments. The group says piracy has drawn international attention, but the suffering of Somali civilians has received far less sustained scrutiny.

The organization is urging the U.N. Security Council to establish a commission of inquiry to investigate serious violations by all parties and identify those responsible. It also calls on governments supporting Somali forces, including the United States and regional partners, to condition assistance on respect for human rights and accountability for abuses.

Somalia has been without a strong central government since 1991, when longtime ruler Mohamed Siad Barre was overthrown. Since then, rival warlords, clan militias, Islamist movements and foreign-backed authorities have fought for power, leaving civilians trapped in cycles of violence, displacement and hunger.

Human Rights Watch says accountability is essential if Somalia is to break that cycle.

“Somali civilians have suffered from years of unlawful attacks and political neglect,” the report says in effect. “Without a serious international investigation, those responsible for the worst abuses are likely to remain beyond reach.”

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a wire-service-style story dated around the Obama transition about Somalia’s conflict, quoting Human Rights Watch’s criticism that U.S. policy has fueled extremism and abuses.
counterfactuals.output:
NAIROBI, Kenya, Jan. 13, 2009 (AP) — As President-elect Barack Obama prepares to take office, human rights advocates are urging his administration to rethink U.S. policy toward Somalia, warning that Washington’s counterterrorism-focused approach has helped deepen the country’s conflict and contributed to abuses against civilians.

Human Rights Watch said in a report released Tuesday that U.S. support for Ethiopia’s 2006 military intervention in Somalia and backing for the country’s weak transitional government had fueled resentment, strengthened Islamist insurgents and left ordinary Somalis exposed to violence by all sides.

“U.S. policy on Somalia has been dominated by counterterrorism concerns and has helped to fuel the very extremism it seeks to eliminate,” the group said. It accused Ethiopian forces, Somali government troops and insurgent groups of committing serious abuses, including indiscriminate attacks, arbitrary arrests and killings.

Somalia has not had an effective central government since 1991. The latest phase of the conflict began after Ethiopian troops, with U.S. support, drove the Islamic Courts Union from Mogadishu in late 2006. The intervention helped install Somalia’s Transitional Federal Government in the capital, but it also triggered a powerful insurgency led in part by al-Shabab, a militant Islamist group with alleged ties to al-Qaida.

Ethiopia has begun withdrawing its forces under a U.N.-backed peace process, raising fears of a security vacuum in Mogadishu and other parts of south-central Somalia. African Union peacekeepers from Uganda and Burundi remain in the capital but are too few to secure the country.

Human Rights Watch called on the incoming Obama administration to break with Bush administration policy by pressing Somali and Ethiopian authorities to investigate abuses, conditioning assistance on respect for human rights and supporting accountability for war crimes.

The group also urged Washington to ensure that counterterrorism efforts do not rely on abusive local partners or sweeping detention practices.

The Bush administration has viewed Somalia largely through the lens of the global fight against terrorism, carrying out occasional airstrikes against suspected al-Qaida operatives and supporting regional allies opposed to Islamist movements. U.S. officials have said the policy is aimed at preventing Somalia from becoming a safe haven for international terrorists.

But aid groups say the fighting has produced one of the world’s worst humanitarian crises. More than 1 million Somalis have been displaced, and millions more depend on emergency food assistance. In Mogadishu, shelling and gun battles have devastated neighborhoods and forced many residents to flee repeatedly.

Somalia’s transitional leaders are struggling to implement a power-sharing deal with moderate Islamists. But al-Shabab and other hard-line insurgent factions have rejected the process and continue to fight for control of the country.

Human Rights Watch said the change in U.S. administrations offers a chance to reassess Washington’s role.

“The Obama administration should make clear that support for Somali authorities and regional partners will not come at the expense of civilians’ rights,” the group said. “Ignoring abuses has only made Somalia’s crisis worse.”
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a CNN.com-style international news piece on the worsening humanitarian situation in Somalia, focusing on Human Rights Watch’s recommendations to Western governments, Ethiopia, Somali authorities, and militias.
counterfactuals.output:
**Somalia’s humanitarian crisis deepens as rights group urges action from Western governments, Ethiopia and armed groups**

*By [Your Name], CNN-style International Correspondent*

Somalia’s humanitarian emergency is worsening as conflict, displacement, food insecurity and climate shocks converge, leaving civilians trapped between armed groups, abusive security forces and a collapsing aid pipeline, Human Rights Watch has warned.

In a new appeal, the rights organization urged Western governments, Ethiopia, Somali authorities and militias operating in the country to take immediate steps to protect civilians and expand humanitarian access, warning that the cost of inaction will be measured in lives lost.

Somalia has faced years of overlapping crises: a long-running insurgency by al-Shabaab, clan-based violence, political instability, and repeated droughts followed in some areas by flooding. Millions of people remain in need of assistance, while hundreds of thousands have been displaced from rural communities into overcrowded camps where food, clean water, shelter and health care are scarce.

Human Rights Watch said civilians are increasingly vulnerable to abuses by all sides, including forced recruitment, indiscriminate attacks, extortion, restrictions on movement and obstruction of aid.

### Call for Western governments to increase pressure and aid

Human Rights Watch urged Western governments — including the United States, European Union members and the United Kingdom — to do more than provide emergency relief.

The group called on them to increase humanitarian funding, support independent monitoring of aid delivery, and ensure assistance reaches communities most at risk, particularly displaced people, women, children and minority clans.

It also urged donor governments to use diplomatic leverage with Somali authorities and security partners to press for accountability for abuses committed by government forces, allied militias and other armed actors.

Western governments that provide security assistance to Somalia should ensure that military aid, training and intelligence support are not enabling units implicated in violations, the group said. It recommended conditioning assistance on respect for international humanitarian law and credible investigations into alleged abuses.

### Ethiopia urged to protect civilians and allow aid access

Human Rights Watch also directed recommendations at Ethiopia, whose forces have played a significant role in Somalia through bilateral deployments and under African Union-backed security arrangements.

The group called on Ethiopian forces operating in or near Somalia to comply with international humanitarian law, protect civilians during military operations, and avoid actions that could worsen displacement or block humanitarian access.

It also urged Ethiopia to ensure that people fleeing violence and hunger are not forcibly returned to unsafe areas. Rights groups have repeatedly warned that border closures, pushbacks or restrictions on refugees can place vulnerable civilians at further risk.

### Somali authorities pressed on accountability

For Somalia’s federal government and regional authorities, Human Rights Watch called for urgent measures to protect displaced communities and end abuses by state-aligned forces and local militias.

The group recommended that Somali authorities investigate allegations of unlawful killings, arbitrary arrests, sexual violence, forced evictions and aid diversion. It also urged officials to improve security in displacement camps, where women and girls are at heightened risk of sexual assault and exploitation.

Somali authorities should also ensure humanitarian organizations can operate safely and independently, HRW said, including in areas affected by military offensives or clan fighting.

The rights group emphasized that counterterrorism operations against al-Shabaab must not come at the expense of civilian protection.

### Militias and armed groups told to stop abuses

Human Rights Watch called on clan militias and other armed groups to immediately stop attacks on civilians, looting, forced recruitment and obstruction of aid.

It urged all armed actors to allow safe passage for civilians seeking food, water and medical care, and to permit humanitarian agencies to reach communities in need.

Al-Shabaab, which controls parts of rural Somalia and frequently targets civilians, government officials and security forces, has long been accused of carrying out bombings, assassinations, forced taxation and recruitment of children. HRW said all armed groups, including al-Shabaab and clan-based militias, must abide by the laws of war.

### A crisis with shrinking attention

Aid agencies have warned that Somalia’s crisis is receiving less international attention and funding than required. Humanitarian needs remain acute, but global donor fatigue and competing emergencies — from Gaza and Sudan to Ukraine — have strained relief budgets.

The consequences are visible in displacement camps, where families often survive on limited food distributions and informal work. Malnutrition rates remain high in many areas, and health workers warn that children are especially vulnerable to disease outbreaks when clean water and sanitation are unavailable.

Human Rights Watch said the worsening situation should be treated not only as a humanitarian emergency, but also as a protection crisis driven by conflict and impunity.

“Governments and armed groups have legal obligations to protect civilians,” the organization said in its recommendations. “Humanitarian aid must be allowed to reach people in need, and those responsible for abuses should be held accountable.”

For many Somalis, the immediate demands are simpler: safety, food, water and the chance to return home. But as violence continues and aid resources dwindle, those hopes are becoming harder to sustain.
